# Overview

The [linear regression vignette](using-rcppensmallen.html) minimized the
residual sum of squares, a problem that also has a closed-form solution.
Logistic regression does not. There is no closed-form formula that returns the
maximum likelihood estimate, so the coefficients have to be found by iteration,
which is the problem [`ensmallen`](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html) is
built to solve.

This vignette develops the solver step by step. Each piece of C++ shown below is
a fragment of one file, and the finished file is included with the package:

```{r example-path, eval = FALSE}
system.file("examples", "logistic-regression.cpp", package = "RcppEnsmallen")
```

The same code is also compiled into the package as `logistic_reg_lbfgs()` and
`logistic_reg_adam()`. Because compiling C++ is slow, this vignette displays
the source without rebuilding it and calls those precompiled functions to
produce the numbers. A third function built on the same objective,
`logistic_reg_lbfgs_path()`, records the points the optimizer passes through
and is developed in
[Watching an Optimizer Run with Callbacks](watching-an-optimizer.html).

# The objective function

The design matrix is $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ with entries
$X_{ij}$, the coefficient vector is $\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$, and the
response is $\mathbf{y} \in \{0, 1\}^{n}$. Indices run $i = 1, \dots, n$ over
observations and $j = 1, \dots, p$ over coefficients, so $p$ is the coefficient
count throughout and fitted probabilities get their own symbol below. An
intercept is a column of ones inside $\mathbf{X}$ rather than a separate term.

The linear predictor $\eta = \mathbf{X}\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ collapses the
$p$ coefficients into one number per observation:

$$\eta_i = \sum_{j=1}^{p} X_{ij}\, \beta_j, \qquad i = 1, \dots, n$$

Each response $y_i$ is Bernoulli with success probability $\sigma(\eta_i)$,
where

$$\sigma(\eta_i) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta_i}}$$

is the logistic function. It acts elementwise, so
$\pi = \sigma(\eta) \in (0, 1)^{n}$ is the vector of fitted probabilities, one
per row of $\mathbf{X}$. In GLM terms this is the mean of the response, the
inverse link applied to the linear predictor.

Each observation contributes the Bernoulli probability
$\pi_i^{\,y_i}\left(1 - \pi_i\right)^{1 - y_i}$, and the responses are
independent, so the likelihood is their product:

$$L(\beta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \pi_i^{\,y_i}\left(1 - \pi_i\right)^{1 - y_i}$$

Taking logs turns that product into a sum, which brings the $n$ contributions
back down to a single number:

$$\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ y_i \log \pi_i + (1 - y_i)\log\left(1 - \pi_i\right) \right] \in \mathbb{R}$$

The coefficients are still hidden inside $\pi_i = \sigma(\eta_i)$. Substituting
the logistic function collapses the two logarithms into the linear predictor and
a single softplus term:

$$\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ y_i \eta_i - \log\left(1 + e^{\eta_i}\right) \right] \in \mathbb{R}$$

Optimizers minimize, so the objective is the *negative* log-likelihood, also a
scalar:

$$f(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ \log\left(1 + e^{\eta_i}\right) - y_i \eta_i \right] \in \mathbb{R}$$

Without indices, the sum over observations is a product with the vector of ones
$\mathbf{1} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, and $\log(1 + e^{\eta})$ acts elementwise on
$\eta$ the way $\sigma$ does:

$$f(\beta) = \mathbf{1}^{\top}\bigl[\log\left(1 + e^{\eta}\right)\bigr] - \mathbf{y}^{\top}\eta \in \mathbb{R}$$

Differentiating with respect to one coefficient at a time gives $p$ partial
derivatives, each of them a sum over all $n$ observations:

$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial \beta_j} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{ij}\left(\pi_i - y_i\right), \qquad j = 1, \dots, p$$

Stacking those $p$ partials into a column is exactly what a transposed matrix
times a vector does, which gives the compact form: the transposed design matrix
times the residual $\pi - \mathbf{y}$ between the fitted probabilities and the
observed responses.

$$\nabla f(\beta) = \mathbf{X}^{\top}\left(\pi - \mathbf{y}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$$

Reading the dimensions of that product, $(p \times n)$ times $(n \times 1)$,
makes the bookkeeping explicit: the sum over $i$ collapses the observation
dimension and leaves a $p$-vector shaped like $\beta$ itself, which is what an
optimizer needs back. The C++ below mirrors this, with `beta` and the gradient
`g` both held as `X.n_cols` by 1 matrices. The steps behind these expressions
are collected in the [derivation](#derivation) at the end of the vignette.

Unlike the linear regression case, setting this to zero does not isolate
$\beta$. That is why we need an optimizer.

# A note on numerical stability

Translating $\log(1 + e^{\eta})$ directly into code is the most common way a
hand-written logistic objective misbehaves. In double precision, $e^{\eta}$
overflows to `Inf` once $\eta$ exceeds roughly 710, so the objective reports
`Inf` even though its true value is very close to $\eta$ itself:

```{r overflow}
eta <- 800
log(1 + exp(eta))   # naive
max(eta, 0) + log1p(exp(-abs(eta)))   # stable
```

An `Inf` here is not usually fatal. The L-BFGS line search fails its acceptance
test on an infinite objective and shrinks the step, so the optimizer backs off
rather than crashing; a `NaN` is the one that stops the search. What you lose is
the *information* in that region. An objective that reports `Inf` instead of 800
cannot tell a line search which of two bad points is less bad, so the search is
steered by a value that no longer separates them. Whether that changes the final
answer depends on the data and the starting point.

The standard fix rewrites the expression so the exponent is never positive:

$$\log\left(1 + e^{\eta}\right) = \max(\eta, 0) + \log\left(1 + e^{-|\eta|}\right)$$

Both sides agree mathematically, but the right-hand side cannot overflow.
Armadillo provides `log1p()` elementwise, which is also more accurate than
`log(1 + x)` when `x` is small.

The logistic function itself needs no special treatment. A very negative $\eta$
sends `exp(-eta)` to `Inf` and the result to 0; a very positive $\eta$ sends it
to 0 and the result to 1. Both are the correct answers, so only the softplus
term needs rewriting.

```{Rcpp helpers, eval = FALSE}
// Numerically stable softplus, i.e. log(1 + exp(eta)), computed elementwise.
inline arma::vec softplus(const arma::vec& eta)
{
    return arma::max(eta, arma::zeros<arma::vec>(eta.n_elem)) +
        arma::log1p(arma::exp(-arma::abs(eta)));
}

// Logistic function, i.e. 1 / (1 + exp(-eta)), computed elementwise.
inline arma::vec logistic(const arma::vec& eta)
{
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + arma::exp(-eta));
}
```

Both helpers are used by the class below: `softplus(eta)` computes
$\log(1 + e^{\eta})$ and `logistic(eta)` computes $\pi$.

# A standalone implementation

Every standalone file using `RcppEnsmallen` opens with the same two lines. The
attribute tells `Rcpp::sourceCpp()` where to find the headers.

```{Rcpp header, eval = FALSE}
#include <RcppEnsmallen.h>
// [[Rcpp::depends(RcppEnsmallen)]]
```

`ensmallen` asks for the objective as a class with member functions of specific
names and signatures. For a differentiable function like this one:

- `Evaluate()`: the value of the objective at the given parameters.
- `Gradient()`: the gradient at the given parameters.
- `EvaluateWithGradient()`: both at once. Optional, but usually faster.

The class below writes `Evaluate()` and `Gradient()` separately, one for each
of the two formulas above.

```{Rcpp classdef, eval = FALSE}
class LogisticRegressionFunction
{
public:
    // Construct the object with the given design matrix, responses, and
    // ridge penalty.
    LogisticRegressionFunction(const arma::mat& X,
                               const arma::vec& y,
                               const double lambda) :
    X(X), y(y), lambda(lambda) { }

    // Return the objective function for model parameters beta.
    // ensmallen passes beta as a p x 1 matrix, one entry per column of X.
    double Evaluate(const arma::mat& beta)
    {
        // The n x 1 linear predictor.
        const arma::vec eta = X * beta;
        // One number: the loss summed over rows, plus the ridge penalty. Its
        // 0.5 is what makes the penalty differentiate to lambda * beta below.
        return arma::accu(softplus(eta) - y % eta) +
            0.5 * lambda * arma::accu(arma::square(beta));
    }

    // Compute the gradient for model parameters beta.
    void Gradient(const arma::mat& beta, arma::mat& g)
    {
        const arma::vec eta = X * beta;
        // Nothing is returned; the p x 1 gradient is written into g.
        g = X.t() * (logistic(eta) - y) + lambda * beta;
    }

private:
    // The design matrix, held by const reference so no copy is made.
    const arma::mat& X;
    // The responses to each data point.
    const arma::vec& y;
    // The ridge penalty applied to every coefficient.
    const double lambda;
};
```

Both functions compute `eta` and then walk over it again. L-BFGS almost always
wants the objective and the gradient at the same point, so the work gets done
twice. Adding `EvaluateWithGradient()` shares one pass between them, and
`ensmallen` will prefer it automatically wherever it helps:

```{Rcpp fused, eval = FALSE}
    // Compute both at once, reusing the single pass over eta.
    double EvaluateWithGradient(const arma::mat& beta, arma::mat& g)
    {
        const arma::vec eta = X * beta;
        g = X.t() * (logistic(eta) - y) + lambda * beta;
        return arma::accu(softplus(eta) - y % eta) +
            0.5 * lambda * arma::accu(arma::square(beta));
    }
```

Supplying all three functions is allowed and is what the included file does.
More detail is available on the
[`ensmallen` documentation page for differentiable functions](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#differentiable-functions).

With the class in place, the exported function picks an optimizer and runs it.
Here that is [`ens::L_BFGS`](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#l-bfgs); the
[optimizer index](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#optimizer-documentation)
lists the alternatives and the arguments each one takes.

```{Rcpp logreg, eval = FALSE}
// [[Rcpp::export]]
arma::vec logistic_reg_lbfgs(const arma::mat& X, const arma::vec& y,
                             const double lambda = 0.0) {

    // Construct the objective function.
    LogisticRegressionFunction lrf(X, y, lambda);

    // Create the L-BFGS optimizer with default parameters. The ens::L_BFGS
    // type can be replaced with any ensmallen optimizer that can handle
    // differentiable functions.
    ens::L_BFGS lbfgs;

    // The objective is convex, so a deterministic start of zeros reaches the
    // same optimum a random start would.
    arma::mat beta(X.n_cols, 1, arma::fill::zeros);

    // Run the optimization.
    lbfgs.Optimize(lrf, beta);

    return beta;
}
```

The linear regression vignette starts L-BFGS from a random draw. Here we start
from a vector of zeros instead, because the negative log-likelihood of a
logistic regression is convex: there is a single optimum, every starting point
reaches it, and starting from a fixed one makes the result reproducible. A
two-dimensional slice of this objective, contoured in
[Watching an Optimizer Run with Callbacks](watching-an-optimizer.html), shows
level sets nested around a single interior minimum.

**Note:** the `// [[Rcpp::export]]` attribute has to appear in the `.cpp` file
Rcpp compiles, but the class does not have to. Moving the class into a header
beside it and including it with `#include` works under both `sourceCpp()` and a
package build. A class used by more than one optimizer usually belongs in a
header. The examples here keep each file self contained so that one file can be
read on its own.

# Running it standalone

Saved as `logistic-regression.cpp`, the file is compiled and loaded with a
single call:

```{r sourcecpp, eval = FALSE}
Rcpp::sourceCpp("logistic-regression.cpp")
```

That defines `logistic_reg_lbfgs()` in the global environment. The remainder of
this vignette instead calls the copy already compiled into `RcppEnsmallen`. The
objective classes there carry the same code as the ones shown here. What the
included files add is scaffolding around them, chiefly a block of `Rcpp::stop()`
argument checks at the top of each exported function. Those checks are omitted
above so the optimizer setup stays in view.

# Verifying the result

Simulating data from known parameters checks two things at once: that the
parameters are recovered, and that an established implementation agrees.
`glm()` maximizes exactly the likelihood we just minimized the negative of, so
the two should agree closely.

```{r data-generation}
set.seed(42)

n <- 5000
beta <- c(-1, 0.7, -0.5, 1.2)
p <- length(beta)

# Design matrix with an intercept column
X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(n * (p - 1)), ncol = p - 1))

# Bernoulli responses with the logistic link
y <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 1 / (1 + exp(-(X %*% beta))))
```

```{r data-estimation}
coefs_ens <- logistic_reg_lbfgs(X, y)
coefs_glm <- glm.fit(X, y, family = binomial())$coefficients
```

```{r comparison-table, echo = FALSE}
compare_coefs <- cbind(beta, coefs_ens, unname(coefs_glm))
colnames(compare_coefs) <- c("Truth", "ensmallen", "glm.fit")
rownames(compare_coefs) <- paste0("Beta", seq_len(nrow(compare_coefs)))
knitr::kable(compare_coefs, longtable = FALSE,
             caption = "Comparison of Estimated Coefficients")
```

The two estimates agree far more tightly than either agrees with the truth. Both
are computing the same maximum likelihood estimate, and the gap to the true
parameters is sampling error, not optimizer error.

```{r agreement}
max(abs(as.vector(coefs_ens) - coefs_glm))
```

# Adding regularization

Maximum likelihood asks only that the coefficients fit the data in front of it.
The objective from earlier is that request written as something to minimize:

$$f(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ \log\left(1 + e^{\eta_i}\right) - y_i \eta_i \right] \in \mathbb{R}$$

Nothing in it prefers small coefficients. When a predictor separates the two
classes the likelihood keeps improving as that coefficient grows, and the
estimate runs off toward infinity.

Regularization adds a second term that charges for size:

$$f_{\lambda}(\beta) = f(\beta) + r(\beta)$$

The first term measures fit and the second measures the coefficients themselves,
so minimizing the sum trades one against the other. The optimizer is unaffected
by the change: it still minimizes a single scalar, and a differentiable $r$
contributes its own derivative to the gradient and nothing else.

Ridge regression takes $r$ to be the squared length of the coefficient vector,
scaled by a chosen $\lambda \geq 0$:

$$r(\beta) = \frac{\lambda}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^{2} = \frac{\lambda}{2}\, \beta^{\top}\beta, \qquad \beta^{\top}\beta = \lVert\beta\rVert^{2}$$

The penalty is an inner product of $\beta$ with itself, $(1 \times p)$ times
$(p \times 1)$, so like the fit term it is one number. Writing both out gives
the penalized objective:

$$f_{\lambda}(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ \log\left(1 + e^{\eta_i}\right) - y_i \eta_i \right] + \frac{\lambda}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^{2} \in \mathbb{R}$$

The first sum runs over the $n$ observations and the second over the $p$
coefficients. Each coefficient carries exactly one penalty term of its own, so
differentiating adds one entry per coefficient and mixes nothing:

$$\frac{\partial f_{\lambda}}{\partial \beta_j} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{ij}\left(\pi_i - y_i\right) + \lambda \beta_j, \qquad j = 1, \dots, p$$

$$\nabla f_{\lambda}(\beta) = \mathbf{X}^{\top}\left(\pi - \mathbf{y}\right) + \lambda \beta \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$$

Both added terms are already in the class above: the
`0.5 * lambda * arma::accu(arma::square(beta))` in `Evaluate()` and the
`lambda * beta` in `Gradient()`. The step from one to the other is in
[the ridge term](#the-ridge-term) at the end.

Larger penalties pull the coefficients toward zero, with the unpenalized
`glm.fit()` estimate carried alongside as the benchmark each column is drifting
away from:

```{r ridge}
lambdas <- c(0, 1, 10, 100, 1000)
ridge_fits <- sapply(lambdas, function(l) logistic_reg_lbfgs(X, y, lambda = l))
```

```{r ridge-table, echo = FALSE}
ridge_all <- cbind(ridge_fits, unname(coefs_glm))
ridge_tbl <- rbind(ridge_all,
                   colSums(ridge_all^2),
                   apply(ridge_all, 2, function(b) max(abs(b - coefs_glm))))
colnames(ridge_tbl) <- c(paste0("lambda = ", lambdas), "glm.fit")
rownames(ridge_tbl) <- c(paste0("Beta", seq_len(nrow(ridge_fits))),
                         "Squared norm", "Max deviation from MLE")
knitr::kable(ridge_tbl, digits = 4, longtable = FALSE,
             caption = "Ridge Shrinkage of the Coefficient Vector")
```

The same numbers read more directly as paths. Each coefficient is pulled toward
zero as the penalty grows, and none of them crosses it:

```{r ridge-plot, parset = list(mar = c(4.1, 4.1, 2.1, 6.4)), fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.2, fig.alt = "Four coefficient paths plotted against lambda on an index axis. Every path moves toward zero as lambda grows from 0 to 1000, with the two positive coefficients falling and the two negative ones rising, and none crossing zero."}
cols <- c("#1b6ca8", "#c0392b", "#2e8b57", "#8e44ad")
matplot(seq_along(lambdas), t(ridge_fits), type = "b", pch = 16, lty = 1,
        col = cols, xaxt = "n", xlab = expression(lambda),
        ylab = "Coefficient", main = "Ridge shrinkage")
axis(1, at = seq_along(lambdas), labels = lambdas)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey70", lty = 3)
legend(par("usr")[2], par("usr")[4], xpd = NA, bty = "n", cex = 0.85,
       legend = paste0("Beta", seq_len(nrow(ridge_fits))),
       col = cols, lty = 1, pch = 16)
```

Lambda is drawn on an index axis rather than a logarithmic one because the
sweep includes $\lambda = 0$, which has no place on a log scale.

`glm.fit()` cannot be asked for the same thing. Its arguments are

```{r glmfit-args}
names(formals(stats::glm.fit))
```

with no penalty, ridge, or `lambda` among them, and `glm()` has none either.
There is therefore no penalized counterpart to set against the fits for
$\lambda > 0$: the `glm.fit` column of the table above holds the unpenalized
estimate, carried across as the fixed reference the other columns drift away
from. It is a like-for-like benchmark only where the penalty is switched off,
at $\lambda = 0$, where the objective is the plain negative log-likelihood that
`glm.fit()` minimizes:

```{r ridge-agreement}
max(abs(ridge_fits[, 1] - coefs_glm))
```

That is the same number the unpenalized comparison printed earlier, because with
$\lambda = 0$ it is the same fit, and it is why the table rounds that column's
deviation to zero.

Penalized GLMs in R normally come from the glmnet package rather than from a
hand-written objective.

The penalty above applies to every coefficient, the intercept included, because
the function has no way of knowing which column of `X` holds the intercept.
Applied statistics normally leaves the intercept unpenalized, since shrinking it
pulls the fitted probabilities toward one half rather than toward the observed
base rate. Adapting the class to skip a designated column is a small change to
both `Evaluate()` and `Gradient()`.

# Scaling up with separable functions

L-BFGS touches all $n$ rows for every step. When that becomes too expensive, the
mini-batch optimizers work from a small sample of rows at a time, but they need
more from the objective than `Evaluate()` and `Gradient()`. A
[*separable* function](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#differentiable-separable-functions)
must also report how many data points it holds and be able to reorder them:

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `NumFunctions()` | How many data points there are |
| `Shuffle()` | Reorder the data between passes |
| `Evaluate(beta, begin, batchSize)` | Objective over one batch |
| `Gradient(beta, begin, g, batchSize)` | Gradient over one batch |

The batch versions take a starting row and a batch length, and return results
for the rows `[begin, begin + batchSize)`. `Evaluate()` returns the **sum**
over that batch, not the mean.

```{Rcpp separable, eval = FALSE}
// The same objective in separable form, which is what the mini-batch
// optimizers require: ensmallen hands it one batch of rows at a time.
// There is no lambda here, so this is the unpenalized negative log-likelihood.
class LogisticRegressionSeparableFunction
{
public:
    // Construct the object, copying the design matrix and responses.
    LogisticRegressionSeparableFunction(const arma::mat& X,
                                        const arma::vec& y) :
    X(X), y(y) { }

    // Return the number of separable functions, one per observation.
    size_t NumFunctions() const { return X.n_rows; }

    // Shuffle the order of the observations.
    void Shuffle()
    {
        const arma::uvec ordering =
            arma::shuffle(arma::regspace<arma::uvec>(0, X.n_rows - 1));
        X = X.rows(ordering);
        y = y.elem(ordering);
    }

    // Return the objective summed over the batch [begin, begin + batchSize).
    // Note this is a sum, not a mean; ensmallen expects the former.
    double Evaluate(const arma::mat& beta,
                    const size_t begin,
                    const size_t batchSize)
    {
        // begin and batchSize index rows of X, so last is the final row used.
        const size_t last = begin + batchSize - 1;
        // batchSize x 1 here, where the full-batch class had n x 1.
        const arma::vec eta = X.rows(begin, last) * beta;
        const arma::vec yBatch = y.subvec(begin, last);

        return arma::accu(softplus(eta) - yBatch % eta);
    }

    // Compute the gradient over the batch [begin, begin + batchSize).
    void Gradient(const arma::mat& beta,
                  const size_t begin,
                  arma::mat& g,
                  const size_t batchSize)
    {
        const size_t last = begin + batchSize - 1;
        const arma::mat XBatch = X.rows(begin, last);
        const arma::vec yBatch = y.subvec(begin, last);

        // Still p x 1: a batch shortens the sum, not the parameter vector.
        g = XBatch.t() * (logistic(XBatch * beta) - yBatch);
    }

private:
    // The design matrix, held by value so that Shuffle() can reorder it.
    arma::mat X;
    // The responses to each data point, likewise held by value.
    arma::vec y;
};
```

There is one structural difference from the full-batch class. `X` and `y` are
stored **by value** rather than as `const` references, because `Shuffle()`
rearranges them in place and cannot do that through a `const` reference.

Running [Adam](https://www.ensmallen.org/docs.html#adam) on this class looks
much like running L-BFGS, with two details that catch people out.

```{Rcpp adam, eval = FALSE}
// [[Rcpp::export]]
arma::vec logistic_reg_adam(const arma::mat& X, const arma::vec& y,
                            const size_t batch_size = 32,
                            const size_t max_epochs = 50,
                            const double step_size = 0.05,
                            const bool verbose = false) {

    LogisticRegressionSeparableFunction lrf(X, y);

    // ensmallen counts iterations in data points visited, so one epoch is
    // nrow(X) iterations.
    const size_t max_iterations = max_epochs * X.n_rows;

    // Arguments are: stepSize, batchSize, beta1, beta2, eps, maxIterations,
    // tolerance, and whether to shuffle between epochs.
    ens::Adam optimizer(step_size, batch_size, 0.9, 0.999, 1e-8,
                        max_iterations, 1e-8, true);

    arma::mat beta(X.n_cols, 1, arma::fill::zeros);

    // Callbacks are passed as trailing arguments to Optimize(). PrintLoss
    // writes to arma::get_cout_stream(), which RcppArmadillo maps to
    // Rcpp::Rcout, so the output is safe to emit from an R package.
    if (verbose) {
        optimizer.Optimize(lrf, beta, ens::PrintLoss());
    } else {
        optimizer.Optimize(lrf, beta);
    }

    return beta;
}
```

`MaxIterations()` counts data points, not epochs or batches. Passing 50 when you
meant fifty passes over the data would stop the optimizer after fifty
*observations*. One epoch is `nrow(X)` iterations, which is why `max_epochs` is
multiplied out above.

Since `ensmallen` 3.10, the SGD family divides the step size by the batch size.
The intent is that batch size and step size can be tuned independently, but it
means a step size carried over from `ensmallen` 2 is effectively `batchSize`
times smaller than it used to be. Defining `ENS_OLD_SEPARABLE_STEP_BEHAVIOR`
before including the headers restores the old behavior.

`ens::Adam` defaults to a step size of 0.001, which predates the change. With a
batch size of 32 that leaves an effective step of about `3e-5`, and the
optimizer stalls far short of the optimum.

The sweep changes the step size and nothing else. Batch size and epoch count
stay at the defaults `logistic_reg_adam()` declares, and every call starts from
the same vector of zeros:

```{r step-size}
set.seed(2024)
step_sizes <- c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.25)
adam_fits <- sapply(step_sizes,
                    function(s) logistic_reg_adam(X, y, step_size = s))
```

```{r step-size-table, echo = FALSE}
step_all <- cbind(adam_fits, unname(coefs_glm))
step_tbl <- rbind(step_all,
                  apply(step_all, 2, function(b) max(abs(b - coefs_glm))))
colnames(step_tbl) <- c(paste0("step = ", step_sizes), "glm.fit")
rownames(step_tbl) <- c(paste0("Beta", seq_len(nrow(adam_fits))),
                        "Max deviation from MLE")
knitr::kable(step_tbl, digits = 4, longtable = FALSE,
             caption = "Adam Coefficients Across Step Sizes")
```

Plotting the deviation against the step size shows both failure modes at once:

```{r step-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.2, fig.alt = "Maximum deviation from the maximum likelihood estimate plotted against Adam step size on logarithmic axes. The curve falls steeply from 0.001, reaches its lowest point at a step size of 0.05, which is circled, and rises again at 0.25."}
dev_from_mle <- apply(adam_fits, 2, function(b) max(abs(b - coefs_glm)))
plot(step_sizes, dev_from_mle, type = "b", pch = 16, log = "xy",
     col = "#1b6ca8", xlab = "Step size",
     ylab = "Max deviation from the MLE", main = "Adam step size")
best <- which.min(dev_from_mle)
points(step_sizes[best], dev_from_mle[best], pch = 1, cex = 2.2,
       col = "#c0392b")
```

Too small a step stalls short of the optimum and too large a one overshoots
it.

This is why `logistic_reg_adam()` defaults to `step_size = 0.05` rather than
adopting `ens::Adam`'s own default.

With a workable step size, Adam lands close to the L-BFGS answer while only ever
looking at 32 rows at a time:

```{r adam-vs-lbfgs, echo = FALSE}
set.seed(2024)
adam_tbl <- cbind(beta, logistic_reg_adam(X, y), coefs_ens)
colnames(adam_tbl) <- c("Truth", "Adam", "L-BFGS")
rownames(adam_tbl) <- paste0("Beta", seq_len(nrow(adam_tbl)))
knitr::kable(adam_tbl, digits = 4, longtable = FALSE,
             caption = "Mini-Batch Adam Against Full-Batch L-BFGS")
```

The Adam column shifts slightly from call to call unless a seed is fixed.
`Shuffle()` draws on Armadillo's random number generator, and `RcppArmadillo`
routes that onto R's own stream, so `set.seed()` makes these results every bit
as reproducible as the L-BFGS ones:

```{r adam-seed}
set.seed(2024); first  <- logistic_reg_adam(X, y)
set.seed(2024); second <- logistic_reg_adam(X, y)
identical(first, second)
```

The flip side is that every call consumes random numbers from R's stream, so it
advances any `rnorm()` or `runif()` draws that follow it.

The `verbose` argument in the function above switches on a callback that
prints the loss after each pass over the data, which turns a run that stopped
short of the optimum into something visible.
[Watching an Optimizer Run with Callbacks](watching-an-optimizer.html) runs
that branch, reads what it prints, and goes on to write a callback that
records the points L-BFGS visits.

# Moving this into an R package

Everything above works from a loose `.cpp` file, but `sourceCpp()` recompiles on
every fresh session. Moving the code into a package compiles it once at install
time, gives the functions manual pages, and lets other packages depend on them.

Three changes carry it across:

1. **Move the file into `src/`.** The `// [[Rcpp::depends(RcppEnsmallen)]]`
   attribute is no longer needed, since `LinkingTo` in `DESCRIPTION` replaces
   it. Keep the `#include <RcppEnsmallen.h>`. This package splits the file in
   three, one exported function each, so each part carries its own copy of the
   helpers inside an anonymous `namespace { }`. The third of them holds the
   callback the other vignette develops, and keeps its copy of the objective
   class in there too, since the L-BFGS file already defines a class of that
   name at namespace scope.
2. **Declare the dependency and build flags.** `DESCRIPTION` needs a `LinkingTo`
   entry, and `src/` needs a `Makevars` and a `Makevars.win`. The
   [package usage vignette](package-usage.html) gives the exact contents.
3. **Regenerate the bindings.** Running `Rcpp::compileAttributes()` writes the
   `.Call()` wrappers into `R/RcppExports.R` and `src/RcppExports.cpp`. Any
   roxygen comments written above the `// [[Rcpp::export]]` attribute are
   carried into `R/RcppExports.R`, so `roxygen2::roxygenise()` will then
   produce the manual page and the `NAMESPACE` export.

Laid out as a tree, and trimmed to the files the move actually touches, that is:

```
RcppEnsmallen/
|-- DESCRIPTION                          # holds the LinkingTo entry from step 2
|-- NAMESPACE                            # export() and useDynLib(); roxygen2 writes it
|-- R/
|   `-- RcppExports.R                    # generated R wrappers around .Call()
|-- src/
|   |-- example-logistic-regression-lbfgs.cpp   # the objective class and logistic_reg_lbfgs()
|   |-- example-logistic-regression-adam.cpp    # the separable class and logistic_reg_adam()
|   |-- example-logistic-regression-path.cpp    # the callback, from the callbacks vignette
|   |-- Makevars                         # compiler and linker flags, Unix-alikes
|   |-- Makevars.win                     # the same flags for Windows
|   `-- RcppExports.cpp                  # generated C++ registration layer
|-- man/
|   |-- logistic_reg_lbfgs.Rd            # generated from the roxygen comments in src/
|   |-- logistic_reg_adam.Rd
|   `-- logistic_reg_lbfgs_path.Rd
|-- inst/
|   `-- examples/
|       `-- logistic-regression.cpp      # the standalone file, kept for sourceCpp()
`-- vignettes/
    `-- logistic-regression.Rmd          # this document
```

Step 1 accounts for the three files under `src/`, and step 2 for `DESCRIPTION`
together with the pair of `Makevars` files beside them. Step 3 accounts for
everything else: `src/RcppExports.cpp`, `R/RcppExports.R`, the pages in `man/`,
and `NAMESPACE` are all generated, so the only hand-written C++ in the tree is
the file you moved.

That is the whole difference between the standalone file and what this package
provides. To compare them directly, the standalone version is at
`system.file("examples", "logistic-regression.cpp", package = "RcppEnsmallen")`
and the package version is split across
`src/example-logistic-regression-lbfgs.cpp`,
`src/example-logistic-regression-adam.cpp` and
`src/example-logistic-regression-path.cpp` in the package sources.

# Derivation

Everything above was asserted rather than shown; here is the algebra in one
place. Throughout, $\eta_i = \sum_{j=1}^{p} X_{ij}\beta_j$, and the vector of
fitted probabilities is $\pi = \sigma(\eta)$ with entries
$\pi_i = \sigma(\eta_i)$. The index $i$ runs over the $n$ observations and $j$
over the $p$ coefficients, and $\nabla f(\beta)$ is a column vector shaped like
$\beta$. Results that have a matrix form are given both ways, with the shape of
each factor carried as a subscript, so that $\mathbf{X}^{\top}_{p \times n}$
marks a $p \times n$ matrix. The index form shows what is being summed; the
matrix form shows what shape comes out.

## From the Bernoulli likelihood to the objective

Independent Bernoulli responses give the likelihood

$$L(\beta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \pi_i^{\,y_i}\left(1 - \pi_i\right)^{1 - y_i}$$

Taking logs turns the product into a sum, and collecting the $y_i$ terms leaves
a log-odds and an offset:

$$\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ y_i \log \pi_i + (1 - y_i)\log(1 - \pi_i) \right] = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ y_i \log\frac{\pi_i}{1 - \pi_i} + \log(1 - \pi_i) \right]$$

The logistic function is built so that both pieces simplify. From
$1 - \pi_i = 1 - \sigma(\eta_i)$ and
$1 - \sigma(\eta_i) = e^{-\eta_i} / (1 + e^{-\eta_i}) = 1 / (1 + e^{\eta_i})$
we get

$$\log\frac{\pi_i}{1 - \pi_i} = \log\frac{1 + e^{\eta_i}}{1 + e^{-\eta_i}} = \eta_i, \qquad \log(1 - \pi_i) = -\log\left(1 + e^{\eta_i}\right)$$

Substituting both gives the log-likelihood used at the start,

$$\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ y_i \eta_i - \log\left(1 + e^{\eta_i}\right) \right]$$

and the objective is $f(\beta) = -\ell(\beta)$.

The matrix form stated earlier is the same expression with every shape carried
along:

$$f(\beta)_{1 \times 1} \; = \; \mathbf{1}^{\top}_{1 \times n}\; \bigl[\log\left(1 + e^{\eta}\right)\bigr]_{n \times 1} \; - \; \mathbf{y}^{\top}_{1 \times n}\; \eta_{n \times 1}$$

Both products run the length of the $n$ observations and return one number,
which is the $1 \times 1$ on the left. In the C++ that $\mathbf{1}^{\top}$ is
`arma::accu()`, which sums `softplus(eta) - y % eta` in a single pass rather
than forming the two products separately.

## The gradient

Only one derivative is needed:

$$\frac{d}{d\eta}\log\left(1 + e^{\eta}\right) = \frac{e^{\eta}}{1 + e^{\eta}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\eta}} = \sigma(\eta)$$

Observation $i$ contributes $\log(1 + e^{\eta_i}) - y_i \eta_i$ to $f$ and
touches no other $\eta$, so

$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial \eta_i} = \sigma(\eta_i) - y_i = \pi_i - y_i$$

The chain rule carries that back to the coefficients. Since $\eta_i$ involves
$\beta_j$ only through the single term $X_{ij}\beta_j$, we have
$\partial \eta_i / \partial \beta_j = X_{ij}$, and every observation contributes
to every coefficient:

$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial \beta_j} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \eta_i}\, \frac{\partial \eta_i}{\partial \beta_j} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{ij}\left(\pi_i - y_i\right)$$

A sum over the *first* index of $X_{ij}$ with the second left free is the
definition of a transposed product: for any $v \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, the $j$-th
entry of $\mathbf{X}^{\top} v$ is $\sum_{i} X_{ij} v_i$. Taking
$v = \pi - \mathbf{y}$ and collecting all $p$ entries,

$$\nabla f(\beta) = \mathbf{X}^{\top}\left(\pi - \mathbf{y}\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$$

The transpose is where the sum over observations went.

The same two steps in matrix form carry the shapes along. Write
$\nabla_{\eta} f$ for the column of partials $\partial f / \partial \eta_i$,
and $\nabla_{\beta} f$ for $\nabla f$ where the two need distinguishing. The
derivative of the linear predictor with respect to the coefficients is the
design matrix itself. The derivative of $f$ with respect to the linear predictor
is the residual $\pi - \mathbf{y}$ between the fitted probabilities and the
observed responses:

$$\left(\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial \beta}\right)_{n \times p} \; = \; \mathbf{X}_{n \times p}, \qquad \left(\nabla_{\eta} f\right)_{n \times 1} \; = \; \left(\pi - \mathbf{y}\right)_{n \times 1}$$

The chain rule composes the two, transposing the first factor so that the index
they share is the one summed over:

$$\left(\nabla_{\beta} f(\beta)\right)_{p \times 1} \; = \; \left(\frac{\partial \eta}{\partial \beta}\right)^{\top}_{p \times n}\; \left(\nabla_{\eta} f\right)_{n \times 1} \; = \; \mathbf{X}^{\top}_{p \times n}\; \left(\pi - \mathbf{y}\right)_{n \times 1}$$

The $n$ sitting on the inside of that product is the observation index, and it
is absent from the result: $(p \times n)$ times $(n \times 1)$ leaves the
$p \times 1$ that `Gradient()` writes into `g`.

## The ridge term

The penalty

$$r(\beta) = \frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\beta\rVert^{2} = \frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^{2}$$

gives each coefficient exactly one term of its own, so

$$\frac{\partial r}{\partial \beta_j} = \lambda \beta_j, \qquad \nabla r(\beta) = \lambda\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{p}$$

The one half in the penalty exists to cancel the 2 brought down by the square,
which is why `Evaluate()` carries a `0.5` that `Gradient()` does not.

Annotating the shapes shows the penalty collapsing to a number while its
gradient keeps the shape of $\beta$:

$$r(\beta)_{1 \times 1} \; = \; \frac{\lambda}{2}\, \beta^{\top}_{1 \times p}\; \beta_{p \times 1}, \qquad \left(\nabla r(\beta)\right)_{p \times 1} \; = \; \lambda\, \beta_{p \times 1}$$

Both terms of $\nabla f_{\lambda}$ are therefore $p \times 1$, which is what
lets `Gradient()` add `lambda * beta` to the vector coming out of
`X.t() * (logistic(eta) - y)` entry by entry.

## The softplus identity

The stable rewrite used earlier,

$$\log\left(1 + e^{\eta}\right) = \max(\eta, 0) + \log\left(1 + e^{-|\eta|}\right)$$

is an exact identity rather than an approximation. The sign of $\eta$ decides
which value $\max(\eta, 0)$ takes and which sign $|\eta|$ strips, so the two
cases are checked separately.

For $\eta \geq 0$, $\max(\eta, 0) = \eta$ and $|\eta| = \eta$, so the right-hand
side is

$$\eta + \log\left(1 + e^{-\eta}\right) = \log e^{\eta} + \log\left(1 + e^{-\eta}\right) = \log\left(e^{\eta}\left(1 + e^{-\eta}\right)\right) = \log\left(1 + e^{\eta}\right)$$

For $\eta < 0$, $\max(\eta, 0) = 0$ and $|\eta| = -\eta$, so the right-hand side
is $\log(1 + e^{\eta})$ with nothing to do.

Both branches return the left-hand side. The difference is what a computer is
asked to evaluate. On the right the exponent is $-|\eta| \leq 0$, so
$e^{-|\eta|}$ lands in $(0, 1]$ and cannot overflow, while the $\max(\eta, 0)$
term carries the large part of the answer exactly.
